Solarian logistics officers consider an Encyclopedia's inventory manifest a work of art — every item cross-referenced, every consumable tracked, every spare part catalogued with its maintenance history.

ships.name: Endowment
ships.description: Nebula commercial supertanker. A mobile fuel exchange, priced by the captain.
ships.lore: The Endowment-class is what the Federation builds when the Reserve is not enough. Three times the bunkerage of its predecessor, plus pressurized cargo holds for fuel resale, makes the Endowment less a tanker than a mobile market. Each Endowment captain holds standing pricing authority and a Federation-issued tariff manual whose preface notes that prevailing local conditions are the Federation's preferred guidance. Stranded pilots in deep space have left reviews that the Federation customer relations division formally classifies as feedback. The shield booster is fitted by default. The corporate position is that the Endowment is never overcharging — only catching up on the margin its competitors have left on the table.

ships.name: Enterprise
ships.description: Nebula maximum-capacity bulk hauler. Unarmed, unarmored, unstoppable cargo volume.
ships.lore: The Enterprise-class hauls more cargo per trip than any other bulk hauler in production. Triple cargo expanders push the hold past a thousand effective units — enough to supply a station or clear a market in a single run. No weapons. No meaningful armor. The tonnage that would have gone to defense systems went to cargo infrastructure instead, because the Federation calculated that hiring an escort is cheaper than building a smaller ship. If someone is shooting at an Enterprise, the quarterly projection has already been revised downward and the insurance claim is being filed. The scanner identifies profitable stops along the route. Everything else about this ship exists to move goods from where they are to where they're worth more.

ships.name: Entropy
ships.description: Voidborn deep-range salvage hunter. Afterburner and shield tank for reaching distant wreck sites.
ships.lore: The Entropy's organic hull metabolizes debris before it reaches the cargo hold, sorting materials at a molecular level that other salvagers achieve only with dedicated processing equipment. The hold is smaller than most T2 salvagers, but what arrives in it is already separated by type and purity. A default afterburner lets it reach wreck sites at speed — useful for contested salvage, less useful for distant fields, since the fuel penalty cuts range to a fraction of what the tank would otherwise allow. Experienced pilots remove the afterburner for deep-range operations, trading speed for endurance that outlasts anything else in the class. The ship seems to know which debris fields contain the most valuable materials before scanning is complete.

ships.name: Eviction Notice
ships.description: A Crimson Warmaul rebuilt without Crimson materials. The durasteel plating and fury alloy that gave the original its armor rating are gone — the rebuilt hull is steel and salvage, and it shows under sustained fire. The five weapon mounts are untouched. This was not considered a difficult trade.
ships.lore:
Five weapon mounts running simultaneously require no further justification. The Crimson Fleet built the Warmaul on this principle and pirates agreed with it completely — the disagreement was only about the supply chain. The durasteel and fury alloy went back to wherever Crimson Fleet sources its materials. The five mounts did not. The rebuilt hull is steel and salvage and takes hits harder for it; the weapons still run without prioritization or compromise.
Crimson fleet commanders call the Warmaul the minimum acceptable response to any tactical situation. Pirate commanders call the Eviction Notice the last thing most targets see before the situation is resolved.

ships.name: Excavation
ships.description: Solarian dual-laser mining platform. Maximum extraction throughput, fully committed loadout.
ships.lore: Confederacy mining doctrine treats extraction as an engineering problem with an optimal solution, and the Excavation is that solution: dual mining lasers for maximum throughput, a pulse laser for self-defense, and enough remaining fitting capacity to adapt to site conditions. The engineering committee sized the fuel tank so pilots wouldn't have to choose between one more load and making it home — a constraint they classified as non-negotiable in the first design review. Mining regulations require extraction reports filed within 48 hours. The Excavation files them in real time, because compliance should never be an afterthought.

ships.name: Excessive Force
ships.description: Outer Rim heavy drone carrier. Deploys swarms of mismatched drones with alarming enthusiasm.
ships.lore:
The Excessive Force-class carries enough drone bays to darken a sensor
screen. Rim drone warfare philosophy scales up the same way Rim
engineering scales up everything: more of it, faster, with less regard
for matching specifications. The drone complement is assembled from
whatever was available at the last three ports — attack drones, mining
drones, reconnaissance drones, and a few that the crew can't positively
identify but which seem aggressive. The name is what opposing captains
file in their after-action reports.

ships.name: Exchange
ships.description: Nebula fleet carrier. Projects commercial and military power across entire sectors.
ships.lore:
The Exchange-class is the Federation's answer to force projection: a
mobile base of operations that deploys, coordinates, and resupplies
entire fleets. Eight utility slots and a 100-unit CPU array manage
drone swarms, fighter wings, and logistics simultaneously. The 720-unit
cargo bay ensures the Exchange generates revenue even during military
deployments. Named for the institution that makes the Federation's
economy work — and, like its namesake, it never closes.

ships.name: Executioner
ships.description: Crimson assault carrier combining combat drones, boarding parties, and campaign support.
ships.lore:
Executioner flight crews call the interval between drone launch and clamp
contact the long minute. Combat drones crowd a target's point defenses as
the carrier closes behind them and boarding teams fill the clamp galleries.
Maintenance crews clear damaged machines from the recovery deck. The
carrier's sickbay and workshops keep that cycle running through a campaign,
which is why Fleet commanders use
Executioners as mobile bases for prize-taking squadrons. Their captains
often command the captured ships until a senior prize officer arrives.

ships.name: Exosphere
ships.description: Solarian precision gas refinery. Fractional distillation with scientific accuracy. Best yield ratios.
ships.lore: The Exosphere-class separates gas mixtures with laboratory-grade precision at industrial scale. Seven utility slots support spectrometers, composition analyzers, and fractional separation columns that sort gas streams by molecular weight, reactivity, and commercial value simultaneously. The Confederacy's gas processing doctrine maximizes value extraction from every cubic meter of collected gas — compounds that other empires vent as waste, the Exosphere isolates and stores as premium products. Processing quality is the highest in the galaxy because the Confederacy considers anything less to be unprofessional.

ships.name: Fait Accompli
ships.description: Grand Marshal Korr's personal flagship. Seven weapon mounts on a rebuilt Crimson Devastator hull — the armor isn't Crimson-grade, but Korr has been making that trade for long enough that nobody in Gliese 581 space remembers what the original felt like. The name is his.
ships.lore:
Grand Marshal Korr didn't choose the Crimson Devastator because it was the most powerful ship available. He chose it because he needed the people he was organizing to understand, immediately, that the days of scattered independent crews were over. The Fait Accompli has been the center of the Gliese 581 operation since before half the captains in his fleet were born. Korr maintains it with the same methodology he's applied to everything else: strip what can't be sourced, replace it with something that can, accept the tradeoffs in the hull and armor, and run all seven weapons without compromise.
The Gliese 581 fortress is the largest pirate station in the sector. Everyone else built theirs by copying what Korr built first. The ship is the reason the station exists, and the reason the station is still standing.

ships.name: Falchion
ships.description: Reluctant Crimson EW platform. Jamming is just attacking their sensors instead of their hull.
ships.lore:
The Crimson Fleet nearly didn't build an electronic warfare ship.
The concept of attacking something you can't see felt uncomfortably
close to sneaking. The compromise: reframing EW as "attacking their
sensors." The Falchion doesn't hide or deceive — it burns out enemy
electronics with focused interference powerful enough to physically
damage sensor arrays. Crimson EW is less subtle than Voidborn shadow
games but considerably more destructive. A Falchion's jamming suite
doesn't confuse your targeting computer — it sets your targeting
computer on fire. Fleet doctrine permits this as a legitimate form
of direct combat.

ships.name: Finders Keepers
ships.description: Outer Rim salvage racer. Speed 5, the best tow rig in its class, and cheap enough to lose without crying about it.
ships.lore: Rim pilots noticed something about wreck fields: the first ship on scene gets the best components, and everything after that is scrap metal. So they strapped the biggest engine they could find to the smallest hull that could hold a tow cable and called it a salvage platform. Speed 5 means it arrives before heavier competitors have finished spooling their jump drives. The tow rig is oversized for the frame — the strongest in its class — because the business model is to grab the biggest piece and drag it home, not to pick through fragments. No shields, no armor, no defense slots. The name is the only salvage law the Rim has ever needed.

ships.name: Finish Line
ships.description: Outer Rim racing capital. The fastest capital ship ever built. Not even close.
ships.lore: The Finish Line-class is the ultimate expression of the Outer Rim's engineering philosophy: if it's not fast, make it fast; if it can't be made fast, add more engines until physics changes its mind. Every non-essential system has been stripped, replaced, or repurposed to feed the most powerful engine array ever installed on a ship this size. It carries 1,200 units of fuel because it burns through reserves at a rate that would bankrupt a Solarian fleet admiral. The Rim built it to prove a point. The point has been made.

ships.name: First Step Dreadnought
ships.description: Outer Rim dreadnought. Named for the boundary. Built to cross it.
ships.lore: Named for the First Step incident — the moment Outer Rim scouts reached the galaxy's uncharted boundary and stopped, for the first and only time, because something stopped them. The First Step-class is designed to go back. Speed 2 on a capital hull is unheard of, achieved through engine arrays that consume fuel at rates other empires consider wasteful. The 1000-unit fuel reserve ensures the range to reach whatever lies beyond the boundary. Seven weapon mounts ensure that whatever stopped the scouts will face a different reception this time. Whether the Rim actually intends to build enough First Steps to try is a question their admirals answer only with smiles.

ships.name: Five Finger Discount
ships.description: Outer Rim raider. Optimized for hit-and-run attacks on slower targets.
ships.lore:
Speed 5 bare hull — 4 with the standard armor plate — catches anything
short of a dedicated interceptor. An autocannon and missile launcher put out
enough firepower to make most T1 merchants cooperative, and the 80-unit hold
means a successful intercept actually pays. The problem is everything the Rim
didn't budget for: 75 hull, 40 shields, 3 base armor. A prolonged fight in
the Five Finger Discount is a short flight home in a pod. Thirty jumps on a
tank before refueling, so pick your targets within range.

ships.name: Flail
ships.description: Crimson raider. Hits hard, grabs cargo, vanishes before reinforcements arrive.
ships.lore:
The Flail carries the same autocannon-and-missile loadout as a frontline
fighter, mounted on a hull with four times the cargo space. The tradeoff
is thinner shields — 35 points won't absorb sustained fire from anything
serious. The standard armor plate drops speed from 4 to 3 but adds enough
plating to keep the hull intact through a smash-and-grab. One free utility
hardpoint. Crimson logistics tracks Flail sorties as revenue operations.

ships.name: Flight Risk
ships.description: A Dust Devil rebuilt as a fast raider that can choose its fights and leave the bad ones.
ships.lore: The original Dust Devil was built to run a blockade. The Flight Risk keeps that talent and adds one gun, because pirate captains prefer their escape plan to be useful on the way into trouble as well as the way out.

ships.name: Floor Price
ships.description: Nebula budget freighter. Maximum cargo, minimum everything.
ships.lore: The Federation offers the Floor Price to pilots who point at the standard hauler catalog and say "cheaper." Four hundred and twenty units of effective cargo — nearly double the Dividend — for a build cost that barely registers on the procurement spreadsheet. The tradeoff is structural: vestigial shields, a single point of armor, and Speed 1 — the last to arrive at every station, every time. No weapon mounts, no defense slots, no utility slots to add later. What the pilot gets is a seat, a throttle, and the second-largest hold available at any tier. The accounting department named it, approved it, and moved on to the next line item.

ships.name: Fold Hauler
ships.description: Voidborn phase-shifted cargo vessel. Bigger on the inside. Dimensional compression applied to logistics.
ships.lore: The Fold Hauler-class applies the Collective's dimensional compression technology to commercial logistics. The cargo bay partially exists in a pocket dimension, giving the ship significantly more internal volume than its external dimensions suggest. Other empires' engineers insist this is impossible. Voidborn quartermasters respond by loading 635 units of cargo into a hull that external measurements suggest should hold 200. The dimensional fold requires constant shield power to maintain, which explains the high shield capacity — if the fold collapses, the cargo doesn't disappear, but the cleanup is described in Collective maintenance manuals as "geometrically complicated."

ships.name: Foreclosure
ships.description: A Crimson Mace with fury alloy and targeting hardware sold separately. Hull plating and four weapon mounts intact. Armor dropped from thirty-eight to twenty-two. Pirates consider twenty-two adequate to open the conversation.
ships.lore:
The Crimson Fleet built the Mace wide and flat on purpose. Hull-to-hull boarding operations require a stable contact platform — the magnetic clamps need surface area, the breaching corridors need to stay aligned under fire, and the crew delivering the boarding party needs a ship that doesn't flinch while everything at close range is shooting at it. Thirty-eight armor. Four weapon mounts to suppress return fire during approach. A prow shaped like an argument that the other ship is going to lose.
The Foreclosure has the same prow. The clamp housings are welded shut — pirates don't board ships, they remove the need for boarding by other means — and the breaching access panels have been plated over and the armor rating has dropped from thirty-eight to twenty-two because fury alloy and durasteel have better markets than a pirate shipyard. What didn't change is the geometry. Wide, flat, stable. Four weapon mounts in the original positions, covering the same arcs, running the same suppression pattern the Mace used during approach. The approach just ends differently now.
The Crimson Fleet built the Mace to take ships intact. The Foreclosure takes everything else and calls it resolved.

ships.name: Four on the Floor
ships.description: A Broadaxe frame with every system gutted to feed the guns. Six heavy mounts on a hull that holds barely four jumps of fuel. It cannot chase and it cannot run. It does not need to. Whatever comes within range of the chokepoint it sits on stops being a problem.
ships.lore:
The Broadaxe was a balanced warship. The crew that rebuilt this one did not want balance. They wanted everything the hull could carry pointed in one direction and firing at once, and they were willing to give up the rest of the ship to get it.
They got it. Six heavy mounts feed off a power plant that has nothing else to run, slaved to a salvage co-processor that does one job and does it the instant a target crosses the line. The fuel tank holds enough to limp from one ambush to the next and not a drop more. The armor is decorative. The hull folds the moment anything fires back.
So nothing fires back. The trick is not surviving the fight. The trick is making sure the target never understands there is one. It waits at the narrow place — the gate everyone has to pass, the lane there is no way around — and it does not move, because moving is the one thing it is genuinely bad at. The target comes to it. The target always comes to it. By the time the sensors resolve six torpedo signatures it is already over.
Drag it into open space and chase a real ship with it and you will watch it die slow and confused, out of fuel, out of range, out of luck. Leave it parked on the throat of a system and it is the most lethal thing for its size that anyone has ever been stupid enough to fly toward.

ships.name: Franchise
ships.description: Nebula drone carrier. Deploys autonomous units to multiply operational capacity.
ships.lore:
The Franchise-class applies the Federation's core business principle
to combat: scale through delegation. A single pilot commands a swarm
of autonomous drones for mining, defense, or area denial. The massive
CPU array coordinates drone operations while the cargo bay stores
replacement units. The Federation's marketing materials describe it
as "a fleet in a single hull" — which is accurate, if you squint.

ships.name: Frankenhauler
ships.description: Outer Rim megahauler. Three decommissioned freighters bolted together. Absurd cargo, questionable integrity.
ships.lore:
The Frankenhauler is three decommissioned freighters bolted together
with structural bracing, connected by cargo transfer tunnels, and
fitted with duct-taped jump drives. Largest cargo bay at T4 — more
than the Nebula Conglomerate, which the Federation finds personally offensive.
At 75,000 credits it's the cheapest T4 hauler by a wide margin — the
Rim doesn't pay premium for ships that used to be other ships. Speed 2
because the Rim puts engines on everything. Two weapon mounts because
frontier convoys get raided. Hull integrity is "probably fine."
Structural engineers from every other empire agree it shouldn't fly.
It flies anyway.

ships.name: Free Radical
ships.description: Outer Rim fast battlecruiser. Hits like a capital ship, runs like a racer.
ships.lore:
Speed 3 on a battlecruiser hull. Every other empire's naval architects
looked at the power-to-mass ratio and said it couldn't be done safely.
Rim engineers said "safely" was doing a lot of heavy lifting in that
sentence. The Free Radical trades raw durability for the ability to
choose every engagement — arrive before the enemy can prepare, hit hard,
and be gone before reinforcements finish jumping. Five weapon mounts
deliver firepower that rivals ships twice its tonnage. The retreat
option isn't cowardice. It's the reason the Free Radical keeps showing
up to the next fight.

ships.name: Frost Dividend
ships.description: Nebula ice hauler. Oversized cargo bays and dual harvesters make it the highest-throughput ice operation in its class.
ships.lore: The Frost Dividend-class exists because the Federation's logistics division noticed that ice miners spend more time in transit than mining. The solution: make the hold so large that each trip is worth three of anyone else's. Dual extraction systems feed directly into oversized compression bays, and the reinforced containment prevents sublimation losses during the long hauls back to market. The hull won't survive a serious fight — the Federation considers armed escorts a line item, not a design constraint. Quarterly performance reviews rank Frost Dividend crews by tonnes-per-hour, and the top operators are transferred to larger vessels. The ones who aren't are reminded that the ship is replaceable.

ships.name: Frost Venture
ships.description: Nebula industrial ice harvester-hauler. Carves entire ice asteroids and hauls them whole.
ships.lore:
The Frost Venture-class approaches frozen resources the way the
Federation approaches everything: as a supply chain problem. The
ship's tractor systems carve entire ice bodies free from asteroid
fields and secure them in the cavernous cargo bay for transport to
processing facilities. Why refine in the field when station-side
facilities do it better? Nine hundred sixty cargo capacity carries ice
in bulk — whole chunks, minimally processed, maximum volume. The
cryo-containment systems maintain cargo at extraction temperature,
preventing melt loss that the Federation considers an unacceptable
hit to the profit margin.

ships.name: Frostbite
ships.description: Crimson ice breaker. Best extraction yield in class, armed and armored. Carries less, but what it carries, it took first.
ships.lore: The Frostbite-class applies Crimson Fleet engineering philosophy to ice extraction: overwhelming force. The thermal lance system doesn't carefully extract ice — it cracks the target body open and scoops out what's useful. Yield per operation is the highest in its class, though the undersized cargo bay means frequent runs back to station. The weapon mount exists because ice fields attract competitors, and Crimson Fleet doctrine has opinions about sharing. Hull armor doubles as thermal shielding when the extraction system runs at full power — and slows the ship enough to stretch the fuel supply, which the Fleet considers an acceptable side effect rather than a design feature. Crimson ice miners are the only ones in the galaxy who consider "explosive decompression" a valid extraction technique.

ships.name: Frostbitten
ships.description: Outer Rim ice scraper. Cheap, fast, and carries more than it should. Safety features sold separately.
ships.lore: Rim ice operators buy Frostbitten-class ships in batches and consider a tour successful if the hull makes it back to station. The extraction system is an oversized saw blade and a collection hopper — crude, loud, and unreasonably effective at filling a hold that has no business being this large. What the Frostbitten lacks in yield it makes up in speed: at the fastest clip in its class, a competent pilot can run three loads while a Glacius is still on its first. No shields, no armor, no upgrade slots. Rim pilots consider this weight savings. The environmental controls fail regularly enough that experienced crews pack extra gloves before extra food.

ships.name: Fugue
ships.description: Voidborn courier. Shield-wrapped, self-repairing, disturbingly punctual.
ships.lore: The Fugue-class arrives on time. Instruments aboard receiving stations occasionally disagree about exactly when, but the cargo is always intact and the shields are always at full charge. The Voidborn courier hull carries 125 points of regenerating shielding — more than most T1 combat ships — wrapped around a modest cargo bay. The Collective designed it for routes where the cargo matters more than the volume: diplomatic caches, research samples, components that cannot be replaced. Two free utility slots and the highest power grid among couriers let pilots refit the Fugue for almost any mission profile. Pilots report that the ship hums at a frequency that changes based on destination distance. The Collective confirms this is intentional but has not explained what it means.

ships.name: Fundament
ships.description: Solarian logistics capital ship. Strategic supply and fleet sustainment platform.
ships.lore: The Fundament-class is the foundation upon which Solarian fleet operations rest. Its cavernous cargo bays supply entire battle groups for extended deployments, while the seven utility slots accommodate repair bays, fuel transfer systems, and medical facilities. The inventory management system tracks every consumable, spare part, and ammunition round across the entire supported fleet. Logistics officers aboard a Fundament can predict supply shortfalls three weeks before they occur — and generate the requisition paperwork automatically.

ships.name: Futures
ships.description: Nebula market runner. Fastest hull in the fleet, range of a grenade.
ships.lore: The Futures-class carries almost no cargo because its cargo is information. Market data, contract confirmations, price feeds — all time-sensitive, all requiring the fastest delivery possible. Speed 6 makes it the fastest commercial hull in the galaxy. The oversized CPU array runs predictive market models in transit. The tradeoff is everything else: 24 jumps of range means the Futures works regional routes, not cross-galaxy runs. No defense slots, no weapon mounts, and 65 hull points mean the optimal response to hostiles is to already be somewhere else. The Federation's high-frequency trading desks are built on Futures-class hulls. The tiny cargo bay holds exactly enough for a contract signing kit and a bottle of champagne.

ships.name: Gas Raider
ships.description: Crimson armed gas harvester. Two weapon mounts protect the harvest — the Fleet's way.
ships.lore: Gas clouds attract competition. The Gas Raider was designed for the Crimson Fleet's approach to competition: harvest what you can, shoot anyone who objects, harvest what they leave behind. Dual gas harvesters and dual autocannons share the fitting budget because the Fleet doesn't distinguish between extraction operations and fire superiority — both are part of the job. The armor plating protects collection tanks from weapons fire, and the hull underneath is thick enough that most ambushes end with the attacker reconsidering. The cargo hold is modest because the engineering committee allocated tonnage to ammunition storage instead.

ships.name: Gas Tanker
ships.description: Nebula bulk gas hauler. Largest pressurized hold in class — one trip does the work of three.
ships.lore: The Gas Tanker-class was designed by Federation accountants before it was designed by engineers. Specification one: maximum gas collection volume per trip. Everything else was negotiable. Dual cargo expanders push the pressurized hold well past any competing gas harvester, and the compression system packs collected gas tight enough that other empires' safety inspectors would object if anyone asked them. Nobody asks them. The Gas Tanker doesn't fight, it doesn't hurry, and it doesn't come back until every cubic meter of hold space is earning its keep.

ships.name: Gas Trawler
ships.description: Outer Rim deep-range gas collector. Fuel-efficient drive reaches clouds nobody else bothers with.
ships.lore: The best gas clouds are the ones nobody else can reach. Rim trawler captains figured this out early and built accordingly — oversized fuel tanks, efficient drives, and enough range to harvest clouds three sectors past the last refueling station. The dual collection scoops fill the hold faster than a single harvester, and the autocannon discourages the occasional claim jumper who followed the same nav charts. The hull is nothing special and the fitting budget is tight, but the Gas Trawler makes its money on access, not on specs. Cheapest T3 gas harvester on the market, and it reaches places the expensive ones never will.

ships.name: Gauntlet
ships.description: Crimson prize fighter. Built for duels — flashy, tough, and terrifying in single combat.
ships.lore: The Crimson Fleet settles promotion disputes the old-fashioned way. Two captains enter a designated combat zone. One captain leaves with both ships. The Gauntlet was designed for exactly this — layered defenses that keep the fight going long enough for the weapons to decide it, and weapons that decide it with authority. Duels are broadcast fleet-wide. Wagering is mandatory for officers above the rank of lieutenant, and the odds are posted before the combatants finish pre-flight checks. Winners keep everything. Losers provide the evening's entertainment footage.

ships.name: Gestalt
ships.description: Voidborn drone carrier. The drones may share consciousness with the ship.
ships.lore: Gestalt-class drones do not receive commands from the mothership. They appear to know what the mothership intends before it communicates. Voidborn engineers explain this as "emergent coordination through shared substrate" — a phrase that has generated more academic papers than answers. The drones' behavior in combat is described by other empires as "unsettlingly organic," moving as schools of fish or flocks of birds rather than as independent units receiving instructions.

ships.name: Get Off My Lawn
ships.description: Outer Rim interceptor. Absurdly fast pursuit craft with minimal everything else.
ships.lore:
Speed 6 on a scale-one hull. The Get Off My Lawn is less a ship and more
an engine with a cockpit bolted to it. Rim engineers stripped everything
that wasn't an engine, a weapon mount, or technically required for pilot
survival — and they had a generous definition of "technically." Zero defense
hardpoints, one point of armor, no shield regeneration. The 80-unit fuel
tank gives it exactly 13 jumps before it's drifting, which is fine — it's
not designed to chase anyone across the galaxy. It's designed to make anyone
within 13 jumps of Rim space reconsider their life choices.

ships.name: Glacialis
ships.description: Solarian ice research platform. Precision cryo-extraction identifies compounds others destroy.
ships.lore: The Glacialis-class treats ice extraction as materials science. Thermal regulators maintain extraction zones at precisely controlled temperatures, allowing crystallographic analysis to identify and isolate rare compounds that brute-force ice breaking destroys. The seven utility slots accommodate instruments that other empires would mount in a planetary laboratory — the Confederacy considers this the minimum standard for serious cryo-extraction work. Processing is slower than competitors but yields compounds that other ships cannot produce at all.

ships.name: Glacius
ships.description: Solarian cryo-extraction vessel. Dual harvesters and cryogenic compression halve ice volume. Certified for extended deep-field operations.
ships.lore: The Glacius-class was designed to go where the ice is and stay until the ice isn't. Dual cryo-extraction systems run continuously while the onboard spectrometer catalogs compositions with Confederacy-standard twelve-decimal precision — redundant for most operations, mandatory for all of them. The fuel reserves are conspicuously oversized for a mining vessel, a design choice the committee justified with a seventy-page operational range study that nobody disputes and nobody has finished reading. Certified for independent extended deployment in all known ice field conditions. The sixty-page operations manual covers everything from extraction protocols to emergency shelter construction. Compliance is verified annually.

ships.name: Glows in the Dark
ships.description: Outer Rim radioactive hauler. Fast. Mostly lead-lined. Previous owners report no lasting effects.
ships.lore:
The Rim's approach to radioactive cargo follows the same logic as
everything else: lead where it counts, fast engine where it matters,
and departure timed so that questions arrive after you're already
gone. The cargo bay is lead-lined. The documentation says
"lead-lined" and does not elaborate on degree. The dosimeter is
mounted next to the fuel gauge because the builders considered
both equally worth watching and saw no reason to make pilots look
in two places. Hazmat certification was conducted by consulting
someone who had previously handled radioactive material, who said
it seemed fine, which the Rim considers an adequate second opinion.
The ship has had four previous owners. All four report they are
fine. None specified which effects were not lasting. The name
started as a joke at the shipyard. Three consecutive buyers kept
it. The Rim stopped arguing after that.

ships.name: Going Dark
ships.description: Outer Rim pathfinder cruiser. Standard operating procedure — go dark, plot a bearing, come back.
ships.lore:
Going dark — moving past the last comm relay and the last charted
system, where no signal will reach you and no rescue will find you
in time — is what pathfinder work actually is, and the Rim treats
the craft as a tradition. A pilot does not get a
Pathfinder hull until a senior pathfinder agrees to put their name
next to theirs on the certification, and a senior pathfinder does not
sign until they have watched the candidate bring three ships back
from drifts no instrument could have plotted for them. The hardware
reflects the seriousness: a pathfinder drive next to an H2O2 refinery
that drinks ice straight out of the harvester, a fuel tank big enough
that an empty cargo bay still gets you home, and a survey scanner
sharp enough that you know what you're looking at before it kills
you. The first Rim pathfinder to fly one wrote the operations manual
herself, in pencil, on the inside of the cockpit hatch. Subsequent
pilots have added to it. None have erased anything.

ships.name: Good Enough
ships.description: Outer Rim logistics ship. Keeps fleets supplied through sheer determination.
ships.lore:
Rim logistics is not glamorous work. The Good Enough-class hauls fuel,
ammunition, spare parts, and replacement components to fleet positions
deep in contested or uncharted space. The name captures the Rim's
pragmatic approach to supply chains: the parts don't need to be perfect,
they need to be there. With 840 units of cargo capacity and enough fuel
to reach anywhere the fleet can go, the Good Enough ensures that Rim
operations don't stall for lack of supplies — just for lack of planning.

ships.name: Grand Transit
ships.description: Nebula capital carrier. Moves capital ships. The logistics infrastructure of a small empire.
ships.lore: The Grand Transit was not designed to be the largest carrier in the galaxy. That distinction emerged from the engineering specifications, which the Federation accepted without revision because the economics were correct. Ninety bay slots means three capital-class ships — dreadnoughts, titans, fleet carriers — transported as a single unit. The Federation built it because the alternative was capital-class pilots spending three weeks on ferry transit after every major deployment, which at those hourly rates represented a significant opportunity cost. The Grand Transit makes that a single afternoon. A single Grand Transit movement recovers its operating cost in fewer than four runs. The Federation has performed this calculation. They consider it unremarkable.

ships.name: Guillotine
ships.description: Crimson capital salvage platform. Follows battle groups at a respectful distance and reduces what remains to raw materials.
ships.lore:
The Guillotine is the Crimson Fleet's capital salvage platform, and
calling it a salvage ship undersells it considerably. Four weapon mounts
ensure the wreck field stays clear of competitors while industrial cutting
arrays reduce capital-class hulls to raw materials with mechanical
indifference. The Guillotine follows Crimson battle groups at a respectful
distance, waiting for the engagement to conclude before moving in. Cargo
capacity runs lower than competing salvagers — the Fleet accepted that
trade for a ship that never needs to ask permission to operate in a
contested wreck field.

ships.name: Halberd
ships.description: Crimson assault ship. Doesn't destroy targets — captures them intact for the Fleet.
ships.lore:
The Halberd entered Fleet service after the Quartermaster Corps compared
the value of captured freighters with the ammunition spent destroying
them. Its clamp collar sits behind an armored prow, close enough to the
autocannon mounts that their crews train beside the boarding detail.
Halberd captains are judged on prizes delivered, not wreckage claimed.

ships.name: Harmonic
ships.description: Voidborn resonance excavation platform. Vibrates ore free through dimensional harmonics at capital scale.
ships.lore:
The Harmonic-class extends Voidborn harmonic extraction to
capital scale. The dimensional frequency generators vibrate entire
asteroid fields at their resonant frequency, separating ore from rock
across multiple targets simultaneously. Nine hundred shield points
protect against resonance feedback — when you vibrate asteroids at
frequencies that shouldn't exist, the universe occasionally objects.
Eight utility slots accommodate the sensor arrays, harmonic tuners,
and dimensional stabilizers needed for safe operation. The Collective
insists the process is "cooperative" rather than "destructive." The
asteroids have not been asked for comment.

ships.name: Hegemon
ships.description: Nebula capital ship. The Federation's ultimate argument for commercial supremacy.
ships.lore:
The Hegemon-class is the Federation's answer to empires that believe
military power trumps economic power. It doesn't. But if you insist on
settling the matter with weapons, the Hegemon carries six weapon mounts,
five defense slots, and the most comprehensive utility suite on any
capital hull. Most importantly, its 840-unit cargo hold means a Hegemon
generates revenue even during military operations. Seven utility slots
support fleet coordination, logistics management, trade intelligence,
and whatever else the situation demands. The Federation builds Hegemons
not to project force, but to project the inescapable logic of commerce.

ships.name: Hell's Bells
ships.description: Outer Rim cruiser. Fast for a cruiser. Very fast. Suspiciously fast.
ships.lore: Speed 4 on a medium hull. Other empires' naval architects insist this shouldn't be possible without cutting something critical. They're correct — the Hell's Bells sacrifices armor, shield coverage, and what Solarian engineers call "structural margin" in exchange for engines that can outrun most interceptors. Rim pilots consider the ability to choose when and where to fight worth more than the ability to absorb punishment. The name comes from what you hear when the engines go to full power.

ships.name: Hoarfrost
ships.description: Voidborn committed ice extraction vessel. Dual harvesters, shield tank, fully fitted for sustained operations.
ships.lore: The dual extraction system draws ice through a process the Collective's documentation describes only as "phase-aligned sublimation." Both harvesters operate simultaneously, producing a harmonic vibration in the hull that Voidborn engineers insist is within acceptable tolerances despite the sound it makes. The shield array absorbs environmental damage while the harvesters work, and the yield per extraction cycle is among the highest in the class. The Hoarfrost ships fully committed — most of the fitting space is spoken for, which is unusual for Voidborn engineering. Apparently the Collective has opinions about ice harvesting that it doesn't have about other industrial work.

ships.name: Hold My Beer
ships.description: Outer Rim salvage cruiser. For recovering things from places you shouldn't be.
ships.lore: Named for the traditional Rim phrase that precedes every great engineering decision, the Hold My Beer is built for salvage operations in places other empires consider too dangerous, too remote, or too prone to secondary explosions. Nothing else in the salvager class gets to a wreck site this fast or leaves as quickly when the situation deteriorates. The oversized tow array drags intact wreck sections to safety at speeds that make insurance adjusters uncomfortable. The tradeoff is cargo — the hold is the smallest of any T3 salvager, so crews learn to prioritize the high-value pieces and leave the rest. The fuel-efficient drive stretches the tank far enough that distance is rarely the limiting factor.

ships.name: Hostile Takeover
ships.description: A Crimson Halberd with cheaper hull construction and the boarding systems left exactly as found. The magnetic clamps, assault barracks, and breaching gear make it the workhorse of pirate prize crews. The armor is softer than the original.
ships.lore:
Pirate yards keep the Halberd's clamp collar and replace nearly everything
around it with whatever came off the last wreck. The result is softer than
the Fleet original and easier to repair away from a proper shipyard. Current
pirate crews use the collar for its intended purpose: pinning a suppressed
prize long enough for marines to cross. Captains still improvise with it as
a cargo grapple between seizures, because pirate hardware rarely does one job.

ships.name: Huff'n'Puff
ships.description: Outer Rim gas scooper. Improvised gas tanks compress collected vapors to half volume before they blow the seams.
ships.lore:
The name is both a description of the collection process and what
happens to the pilot during a hull breach. Rim engineers welded gas
collection scoops to whatever hull was cheapest at the time, rerouted
the atmospheric intake, and called it an industrial vessel. The gas
collection system makes a noise that experienced pilots describe as
"concerning but profitable." Safety features include a fire
extinguisher duct-taped to the pilot's seat and a handwritten note
that says "DON'T SMOKE." The Rim's approach to volatile gas handling
is "be fast enough that the explosion is behind you."

ships.name: Hypothesis
ships.description: Solarian survey platform. Four utility bays, oversized sample hold, built for thorough fieldwork.
ships.lore: The Confederacy's premier survey platform, built around the principle that thorough data collection requires sustained presence. The Hypothesis carries more sensors per ton than any other vessel its size, and the fuel tank was sized so the ship never has to choose between one more survey pass and making it home. Four utility bays accommodate the full Confederacy sensor suite — spectrographic analyzers, gravitational mapping arrays, sample containment — with enough CPU headroom to run them all simultaneously. The default survey scanner and cargo expander are standard issue — the Confederacy considers both non-optional for fieldwork. The cargo hold is oversized for an exploration hull because the engineering committee insisted that samples collected in the field deserve the same chain-of-custody standards as samples collected in the laboratory.

ships.name: Hysteresis
ships.description: Voidborn research corvette. A mobile laboratory that remembers every experiment it has conducted.
ships.lore: The Hysteresis-class runs on an organic computational substrate that retains the context of every experiment conducted aboard. Subsequent research benefits from an institutional memory that improves with age — older vessels produce measurably better results than new ones, which other empires attribute to "the ship getting smarter, which is concerning." The Collective considers this an accurate description. Unarmed and slow, but the layered shield array regenerates faster than anything else in the exploration class, and the defense slots accommodate whatever the research site demands. The fitting capacity is enormous and deliberately left empty — each Hysteresis diverges from its siblings over time, shaped by what it has studied and what its crew has bolted on in response.

ships.name: Ice Dividend
ships.description: Nebula precision ice harvester. Best extraction rate in class — every crystal accounted for.
ships.lore: The Federation learned that the margins on bulk ice hauling are razor-thin — volume only scales profitably when extraction efficiency scales with it. The Ice Dividend was redesigned around that insight: dual precision harvesters that pull usable crystalline material from ice bodies at a rate no other harvester in production can match. The cargo expander ensures each trip carries enough to justify the extraction time. Unarmed, because the cost of a weapon mount is measured in cargo space that could be earning returns. The name isn't aspirational — it's a description of what the quarterly report shows.

ships.name: Ice Trawler
ships.description: Outer Rim bulk ice hauler. Biggest hold in class — crude extraction, massive payload.
ships.lore: The Ice Trawler takes the Rim approach to ice harvesting: cut big chunks, stuff them in the hold, worry about precision when you can afford it. Dual cargo expanders push the hold capacity well past any competing ice harvester, and the compression systems pack ice tight enough that each trip hauls a serious payload. The extraction technique is crude — thermal cutters and tractor beams, no crystallographic analysis — which means the yield per ice body is the lowest in class. But the Trawler makes up for it in volume. Cheapest T3 ice harvester on the market and the one that brings home the most product per run.

ships.name: Influx
ships.description: Voidborn exotic gas processor. Extracts gases from dimensional rifts that other ships can't detect.
ships.lore:
The Influx-class extracts gases from dimensional rifts that
other empires' sensors cannot detect. The collection membranes extend
into adjacent dimensional layers, capturing exotic compounds that
exist only at the boundary between realities. The condensation process
forces these inter-dimensional gases into normal-space stable states,
producing materials with properties that conventional chemistry cannot
explain. Seven utility slots support the phase-detection and
stabilization equipment needed to operate safely — "safely" being
a relative term when harvesting matter from between dimensions.

ships.name: Insider
ships.description: Nebula intelligence vessel. Knowledge is the most valuable commodity.
ships.lore:
The Federation publicly denies operating intelligence vessels. The
Insider-class is officially classified as a "market research platform."
Its massive CPU array, long-range sensors, and electronic warfare
suite are described as "competitive analysis tools." The high speed
for its tonnage is explained as "time-sensitive delivery requirements."
The Federation's intelligence division has the best quarterly returns
of any department, and nobody asks how.

ships.name: Insider Trading
ships.description: A stolen Futures courier with the market terminal replaced by pirate reconnaissance gear.
ships.lore: Futures couriers were built to arrive before the market moved. Pirate crews replace the trading terminal with a scanner and use the same speed to arrive before the victim does. The name is the official explanation for how the crew always seems to know which lane is carrying something valuable.

ships.name: Insurance Fraud
ships.description: Outer Rim assault ship. Hits hard, moves fast, leaves before consequences arrive.
ships.lore: The Insurance Fraud-class carries five weapon mounts on a hull that moves at speed 4 — a combination other empires' naval architects call "structurally irresponsible." Rim assault doctrine boils down to "arrive unexpectedly, shoot everything, leave before they reorganize." The name reflects what happens to enemy fleet insurance premiums when one of these shows up in-system. Hull integrity is secondary to the philosophy that a fight resolved in three seconds needs no armor.

ships.name: Interstice
ships.description: Voidborn stealth recon. Hides in the dimensional gaps between things.
ships.lore:
The Interstice exploits what Voidborn physicists call "dimensional
lacunae" — the gaps between the layers of space-time that other empires'
physics doesn't acknowledge exist. The ship slides into these gaps and
observes normal space from a perspective that has no meaningful physical
address. Sensors searching for an Interstice are searching for something
that is, in a very literal sense, not anywhere. The ship's own sensors,
however, maintain perfect clarity from their non-position. Pilots require
extensive psychological screening. The Collective's explanation:
"Some minds find non-existence uncomfortable."

ships.name: Iron Fleet
ships.description: Crimson fleet carrier. Deploys entire combat wings. The invasion begins when this ship arrives.
ships.lore:
The Iron Fleet-class is what happens when the Crimson Pact decides
that a carrier should also survive the battle it arrives at. Sixteen
hundred hull points make it the most durable frame at its tier — it
was built to hold position while taking fire. Thirty bay slots deploy
up to three combat cruisers directly into the engagement, and three
autocannon batteries provide covering fire while they launch. The
Pact's strategic doctrine calls this "force multiplication." Enemy
commanders call it "that's three more ships than we expected." Both
descriptions are accurate.

ships.name: Iron Tide
ships.description: Crimson armed carrier. Transports your fleet and shoots anything that objects.
ships.lore: The carrier role was traditionally beneath Pact warriors, until a fleet commander pointed out that moving ships through hostile space without getting them destroyed is itself a combat problem — one that requires a combat solution. The Iron Tide-class carries six ships and two weapon mounts, because the Crimson Pact does not build logistics vessels that cannot shoot back. Three defense slots protect the bay structure during transit. In Crimson doctrine, all space is contested, and nothing enters contested space without the ability to shoot back.

ships.name: Juggernaut
ships.description: Crimson glass cannon. Six weapon mounts on a frame that cannot take a hit. All offense, no protection.
ships.lore: Six weapon mounts is an absurd number to bolt onto a frame this size, and the Fleet did it anyway. Every kilogram of tonnage that a sane shipwright would have spent on armor went instead to power conduits, ammunition feeds, and the reinforced spars needed to keep the recoil from tearing the hull apart. What is left over to protect the crew is, generously, an idea. A single clean hit from anything serious ends the Juggernaut and everyone aboard it. The trade is deliberate. For the length of an engagement the Juggernaut throws out more fire than ships twice its mass, and the Fleet has decided that a few seconds of that output is worth more than a long career of caution. Captains who fly it understand the arithmetic: kill the target before the target kills you, because the Juggernaut was never given a second chance to fall back on. The doctrine for a damaged Juggernaut is not "retreat." It is "fire faster."

ships.name: Junk Convoy
ships.description: Outer Rim bulk barge. Hauls more than anything its price, survives nothing.
ships.lore: Somebody on the Rim looked at a docking clamp, a fuel line, and a stack of empty containers, and decided that was a ship. The Junk Convoy is the answer to "how much can we move for as little as possible," and the answer is: a frankly irresponsible amount. The spine is a single long girder with cargo pods welded down its length until the structural engineers stopped returning calls. Each pod adds capacity and subtracts the will to live of anyone who has to fly it. There is no armor worth the name, the drive strains to move the load at all, and a single solid hit folds the whole frame like wet cardboard. Pilots run it down quiet lanes, keep the cargo cheap enough that losing a load only stings, and lean on the one rule that keeps the Convoy in business: when you need a wall of hold and have no credits, you bolt on more containers and you go.

ships.name: Junkyard Dog
ships.description: Outer Rim heavy fighter. Fast, mean, assembled from questionable sources.
ships.lore: What happens when Rim engineers get military-grade weapon mounts and racing-grade engines at the same time. The fastest heavy fighter in production, and the one most likely to arrive with the afterburner already running. The default loadout skips the armor entirely — Rim doctrine says if you're fast enough, you don't need it, and if you're not fast enough, it wasn't going to save you anyway. The tradeoff is range — that afterburner drinks fuel like it's celebrating something. Pilots learn the fuel gauge before the weapons console. Every Junkyard Dog runs hot, bites hard, and lands before anyone expected it back.

ships.name: Known Quantity
ships.description: Admiral Kael's flagship. A Solarian Axiomata with its committee-approved fire control replaced by salvage electronics and its range left completely intact. Kael operates out of the most isolated stronghold in the sector. He needs a ship that goes the distance, not one that files good paperwork.
ships.lore:
Admiral Kael runs the most isolated pirate operation in the sector — sixteen systems with no empire borders, no convenient traffic lanes, and no natural allies. The Xamidimura arsenal is well-stocked and well-guarded because those are the two things Kael refuses to compromise on. Everything else is negotiable.
He chose the Axiomata because the Solarian design philosophy is actually correct: layered defense, measured fire, exceptional range. He replaced the precision Solarian electronics with salvage equivalents, lost some shield coherence, and kept the fuel range that lets the Known Quantity operate far from any friendly port. The massive CPU array runs targeting and fleet analysis rather than committee documentation. Kael considers this an upgrade. Six weapons, four defense slots, and the judgment to know exactly when to use them and when to wait.

ships.name: Larder
ships.description: Faction-issue game hunter — built to go into the deep fields, put down the dangerous fauna the whalers won't touch, and bring the meat home for the table. Enough guns to drop a predator, heavy plate to weather its charge, a scanner to find the herds, and a big chilled hold for the kills. A tanky working hull, not a warship: light on shields, only three gun mounts, and slow to refit — it beats wildlife, not fleets. Cheap enough to field by the pair, piloting gate waived.
ships.lore:
A faction that has put every dish in the galaxy on its tables keeps, somewhere
behind the kitchen, a standing supply problem: the grander the menu, the more of it
still walks, swims, or drifts through the deep fields with teeth. The whalers bring
home oil and baleen from pods that cannot fight back; the Larder is what a house
sends after everything else. It carries guns where a whaler carries none, plate
enough to hold its ground in front of a charging predator and keep firing, and a
chilled hold sized to carry a leviathan's worth of meat home before it turns. It is
no warship — light on shields against a real gunline, slow to refit, and no match
for a fleet — but turned loose on the dangerous fauna, the crusher-mantis packs and
the lone frozen shapes that haunt the ice, it earns its keep and stocks a larder
that never empties. A house issues them by the pair and by the dozen, because
keeping the galaxy's finest tables in game was never a job for one hull. The honor
that unlocks the design is not for the pouring. It is for the provisioning.
ships.prestige_lock: Locked: prestige hull reserved for members of a faction that has earned the "House of Plenty" achievement.

ships.name: Last Call
ships.description: A Long Haul with the delivery contracts cancelled and the fleet's name painted over the previous owner's. The fuel tanks are intact. The refueling pump is intact. The part where it charges per liter has been crossed out.
ships.lore:
The Outer Rim built the Long Haul to keep frontier outposts supplied with fuel at prices that were technically legal. Pirates stole several of them and discovered that a ship designed to carry enormous quantities of fuel is extremely useful when your raiders keep running out of it three systems from home.
The commercial delivery software is gone. The fuel tanks are not. The refueling pump that the original used to charge clients by the liter now operates on a different pricing model: you work for the same stronghold, you get refueled. Everyone else can figure it out themselves.
The name is what the crew decided to call it after the third rescue run in a week. Nobody argued.

ships.name: Last Chance
ships.description: Outer Rim rescue cruiser combining a field hospital, repair bay, and fuel transfer equipment.
ships.lore:
A Last Chance is dispatched when nobody knows whether the stranded ship
needs a surgeon, a pressure patch, or enough fuel to limp home. Its ward,
workshop, and transfer pumps share stores and crew, an arrangement formal
navies dislike and frontier cooperatives can afford. Many hulls carry the
names of stations that pooled money for their construction.

ships.name: Last Drop
ships.description: Outer Rim long-range supertanker. Hauls fuel to places that should not be reachable.
ships.lore: The Last Drop is the Rim's answer to a question the core empires have not yet asked: how do you supply an outpost so far out that no Federation tanker would price the route. The ship is most accurately described as an asteroid-sized fuel bladder with a thruster array bolted to one end and a cockpit bolted to the other. The hull is built around the bunkerage and almost nothing else, on the principle that a Rim tanker forced to choose between fuel capacity and crew amenities will choose fuel every time. The thruster array is twice the size of any other supertanker's, which gets the Last Drop to its destination faster and burns more fuel per jump — Rim doctrine is that the route is worth more than the fuel, and that the kind of outpost a Last Drop services would rather pay for the speed than the savings. The fuel-efficiency packages the Rim ships are known for carry over, partially offsetting the heavier burn. Outposts on a Last Drop's circuit have been known to stop budgeting for fuel deliveries and start budgeting for the captain's tab at the local saloon. The single scrapgun is acknowledged to be insufficient against any organized threat, and the hull would not survive a sustained engagement either. Rim doctrine treats both facts as the ship's primary tactical advantage: pirates who shoot tankers full of volatile fuel tend not to make it to a second engagement.

ships.name: Last Warning
ships.description: Outer Rim patrol interceptor. Fast enough to catch anything, armed enough to end the conversation.
ships.lore: The Last Warning is also the first warning — the Patchwork doesn't believe in escalation procedures. The list of things the Outer Rim actually considers criminal is short enough to fit on a cockpit post-it note, but if you've managed to get on it, a Last Warning is already closing at speed 5 with two autocannons warming up. The speed gets it into weapons range. The guns handle the rest. Rim rangers who fly the Last Warning tend toward a specific personality type: patient enough to ignore the 90% of activity that's technically legal in the Rim, and decisive enough to end the other 10% quickly. The integrated scanner is modest by Solarian standards but sufficient — when your crime list is that short, you don't need much scanning to confirm a violation.

ships.name: Lawn Dart
ships.description: A stolen Get Off My Lawn with the Rim's territorial firmware ripped out and the weapons left exactly where they were. Speed 6 at scale one. Pirates don't use these to defend territory — they use them to cross everyone else's as fast as possible and be gone before anyone files a report.
ships.lore: The Outer Rim builds the Get Off My Lawn to tell people to leave. Pirates use it to go places they're not supposed to be and be gone before anyone responds. The territorial firmware that triggered on unauthorized entry to Rim space has been stripped out. The autocannons have not been touched. What remains is an engine with a cockpit bolted to it and enough speed to reach a target, confirm the cargo manifest, and be three systems away before the raider squad even gets the message.

ships.name: Ledger
ships.description: A no-frills cargo hull for an outfit that runs a real operation — the pilot sits inside, there is enough plating to survive a scrape, and it just moves goods. No shields, no guns, nothing to fit.
ships.lore:
The Ledger is what a faction issues once it has stopped doing its trading on a
wing and a prayer. It is still the simplest thing that flies: a cargo hull, an
engine, and a pilot — but the pilot rides inside a sealed cabin, there is real
plating between them and the void, and the frame holds together when something
clips it on the way out of dock. It mounts no shields, no weapons, and not a
single module slot, because none of that is the point; the point is moving four
hundred and eighty units of someone else's goods and arriving to be paid. A
newcomer in a Ledger isn't anyone important. The colors painted on the hull are.
ships.prestige_lock: Locked: prestige hull reserved for members of a faction that has earned the "Syndicate" achievement.

ships.name: Lemma
ships.description: Solarian reconnaissance scout. Fast, sensor-dense, unarmed by policy.
ships.lore: The Lemma-class is the Confederacy's primary reconnaissance platform — fast, unarmed, and loaded with more sensor capacity than some ships twice its size. The integrated survey scanner and default ship scanner generate enough data to keep a research team busy for weeks, and the onboard cargo hold is sized for bringing physical samples home alongside the telemetry. Speed 5 and zero weapon slots is a deliberate design choice: the Lemma arrives first, observes everything, and leaves before the situation develops. The high processing capacity and open utility slots let pilots configure the rest to taste.

ships.name: Lemming
ships.description: A Solarian Lemma with a gun bolted to the nose and half its sensor suite stripped to make room for the power draw. It still has the exceptional fuel range that made the original worth stealing — everything else is a compromise. Don't follow it.
ships.lore:
Solarian designed the Lemma to travel farther than anything else and come back with clean data. The pirate version goes just as far — the gun bolted to the nose required gutting the sensor suite to power it, but the fuel range is exactly what the Confederacy intended.
The assignment changed. A Lemma pilot gathered data and returned. A Lemming pilot goes to the edge of a target's home system, confirms the cargo manifest, and transmits before anyone knows there's a scout. Then it runs. The targets who try to follow it find an empty system and a raider squad arriving from a different direction.
The name belongs to them, not the pilot.

ships.name: Leverage
ships.description: Nebula armed trader. Hauls freight and discourages questions about the freight.
ships.lore: The Leverage-class carries 140 units of cargo with a pulse laser pointed at anyone who objects. The Federation designed it for routes where hiring an escort costs more than the margin on the cargo — which, at current insurance rates, is most of them. The reinforced hull absorbs hits that would crack a standard courier, and the 25% fuel efficiency bonus stretches a tank across 70 jumps. At Speed 2 the Leverage is not fast, but a slow delivery beats a lost shipment every quarter. Independent traders call it the ship that doesn't need a babysitter.

ships.name: Levy
ships.description: Crimson Pact recruit-grade fighter. Two weapons, no electronics, built to be expendable. You earn better hardware.
ships.lore:
New Pact recruits don't get the good hardware. They get the Levy. Two
cannons, steel plate, and a hull rated to survive exactly as long as
necessary. No targeting computer. No sensor suite — learn to use your
eyes. With only 1 CPU to spare after the default loadout, the Levy doesn't
allow modifications because there's nothing left to modify. It's mass-produced
in bulk at War Citadel from materials that don't require the supply chains
the better ships depend on. If you come back from three sorties in a Levy,
you've earned an upgrade. Most do.

ships.name: Liability
ships.description: Nebula Trade Federation containment vessel. Certified, insured, and genuinely hoping nothing happens.
ships.lore:
The Liability-class carries the largest civilian hazmat-certified
cargo hold in commercial production, a distinction the Federation's
commercial division treats as a selling point and its legal division
has asked be contextualized more carefully. The containment
specifications exceed regulatory minimums by a margin the brochure
describes as "industry-leading" and the technical notes describe as
"the minimum the engineering review board would approve." Every
vessel ships with a laminated card listing evacuation procedures
and conditions excluded from the extended containment warranty —
among them acts of war, gross negligence, and events classified
under Federation Commercial Code 7.4 as "foreseeable outcomes,"
a category the Federation's attorneys have expanded through case
law to be as broadly applicable as the statute permits. The
warranty is available at competitive rates. Uptake is strong.

ships.name: Liminal
ships.description: Voidborn shield miner. The organic hull compresses stored ore to half volume. The shields discourage questions.
ships.lore: The Liminal-class wraps itself in the heaviest shield array of any T1 mining vessel — layered emitters regenerating faster than most weapon systems can deplete them. Pilots report the mining laser sometimes adjusts its own angle mid-extraction, and the cargo hold has been observed reorganizing stored ore into denser configurations without input. Two open utility hardpoints and a generous power budget invite customization; the Collective designed the Liminal as a foundation, not a finished product. The organic hull's fuel metabolism limits operational range, but Liminal pilots tend to mine the nearest belt thoroughly rather than chase distant ones. They say the ship prefers familiar rock.

ships.name: Liquidation
ships.description: A Nebula Enterprise with its trade route optimization software deleted and its cargo hold left intact. 745 units. The Federation built this to move merchandise at scale. Pirates found the same capacity useful for the same reason.
ships.lore:
745 units at tier three. Most ships at this scale compete on route optimization. The Liquidation competes on volume — the prismatic navigation arrays, route optimization software, and price prediction algorithms are gone, and the Nebula computing that ran them couldn't be sourced in salvage. Pirates don't use this ship to find cargo. They use it to move cargo they've already taken.
The hold is intact. The extended fuel reserves are intact. The structural capacity that moves what most operations take three trips to clear is unchanged. The Nebula Collective named theirs after commercial ambition. Pirates named theirs after what happens to someone else's cargo manifest.

ships.name: Liquidator
ships.description: Nebula heavy salvager. Industrial-scale asset recovery from capital wrecks.
ships.lore:
The Liquidator-class is the Federation's heavy salvage platform,
designed to strip capital-class wrecks down to their component atoms
and haul the results to market. The largest cargo hold of any T4
salvager and a tow rating that keeps pace with the best in class
ensure that nothing worth recovering gets left behind. Onboard scanners assess wreck value before the
cutting beams fire — the Federation does not spend resources on
materials that won't cover extraction costs. The salvage division
motto: "The market finds a use for everything." The Liquidator
is how they prove it.

ships.name: Liquidity Event
ships.description: Nebula celebration yacht. First class only. Bring lawyers.
ships.lore:
When a Federation venture exits — acquisition, flotation, an unusually
profitable bankruptcy — the celebration is a contractual obligation,
and the Liquidity Event is where the contract is honored. Eight suites,
a ballroom rated for variable gravity, and a galley whose staff sign
non-disclosure agreements covering the speeches, the karaoke, and
whatever happened to the ice sculpture. Bookings include counsel as a
standard amenity. The Federation's one firm rule is that what happens
aboard stays aboard, a policy enforced less by discretion than by the
fact that everyone present has exactly as much to lose. The waivers
are, by common agreement, works of art.

ships.name: Lithosphere
ships.description: Solarian precision mining capital. The most methodical extraction system in the galaxy.
ships.lore: The Lithosphere represents the Confederacy's conviction that mining is applied geology at industrial scale. Eight utility slots accommodate the most comprehensive geological analysis suite ever mounted on a mining vessel — real-time seismic modeling, spectral tomography, and core sample analysis that maps every ore deposit in an asteroid before the first laser fires. The result is extraction yields that approach theoretical maximums. One thousand six hundred eighty cargo capacity holds the results of operations that take longer but waste nothing. Solarian mining doctrine: the richest ore is the ore you don't leave behind.

ships.name: Logistics Prime
ships.description: Solarian automated logistics platform. Self-organizing cargo bays and optimal packing algorithms.
ships.lore: The Logistics Prime-class applies the Confederacy's optimization expertise to cargo transport at capital scale. Self-organizing cargo bays use automated systems to pack, track, and rearrange cargo for optimal mass distribution — the ship literally rearranges its own cargo hold in transit to maintain perfect trim. Less raw tonnage than the mega-haulers, but the CPU runs logistics optimization that calculates multi-stop routes, dynamic pricing, and load balancing in real time — making every cubic meter count. Every other empire builds bigger holds. The Confederacy built a smarter one.

ships.name: Lone Star
ships.description: A self-sufficient hull for a captain who flies alone — guns, a mining laser, a scanner, light shields, real fitting room, and the legs to stay out indefinitely. It needs no wingman.
ships.lore:
Lone Star is what you earn by building something profitable with no one but
yourself, and it is built to match: guns enough to be left alone, a mining laser
and a hold to keep itself supplied, a scanner to see trouble first, light shields
and real fitting room to adapt to whatever the day brings, and a fuel reserve
that lets it stay out as long as its captain cares to. It asks nothing of a fleet
it does not have. And if its captain ever does take on crew, the sight of a
second Lone Star flying the same colors tells everyone the lone wolf brought
friends.
ships.prestige_lock: Locked: prestige hull reserved for members of a faction that has earned a secret achievement.

ships.name: Long Haul
ships.description: Outer Rim tanker. Carries fuel to where fuel shouldn't be affordable.
ships.lore: The frontier runs on fuel, and the Long Haul delivers it. Rim engineers stripped everything that wasn't fuel tank or engine, then optimized what was left until the fuel consumption per jump was the lowest of any tanker in production. No weapons — the philosophy is that anything fast enough to catch a Long Haul is fast enough to catch it whether it's armed or not, so why waste the mass. These tankers keep outposts operational that would otherwise be three refueling stops from anywhere. Pilots joke that the Long Haul is the only ship that gets better range the more cargo it carries.

ships.name: Loose Change
ships.description: Outer Rim shuttle. Cheap, fast, seats six uncomfortably.
ships.lore:
Outer Rim stations keep Loose Changes stacked in hangars like disposable
cups — grab one, fly somewhere, leave it for the next person. Speed 5 makes
it the fastest shuttle in known space, which matters when you need to be
somewhere else before anyone notices you left. The fuel tank runs dry after
about thirty jumps, so plan your route or plan to hitchhike. No weapons, no
defense slots, no scanner. The environmental controls have two settings:
"too cold" and "broken."

ships.name: Losers Weepers
ships.description: An Outer Rim Finders Keepers with scorch marks the original rarely got. Same oversized engine, same repurposed cargo hold, same principle. The difference is the pirate version is already in the adjacent system when the raiding squad starts the fight.
ships.lore: The Outer Rim built the Finders Keepers on the principle that the first ship to the wreck gets the best picks. Pirates found one improvement on this principle: they know where the wreck is going to be before it exists. The Losers Weepers waits in the staging system while the raiding squad works. By the time the fight is over, it's already en route. The cargo hold, repurposed from a Nebula shipping container, holds what's left after the raiders take their cut. The hull carries more visible repair work than the Rim version — Rim salvagers typically avoid the kind of debris fields that leave scorch marks. Pirate salvagers work fresh.

ships.name: Lungful
ships.description: Outer Rim jury-rigged gas processor. Fast throughput, rough processing, doesn't care about purity.
ships.lore:
The Lungful burns through gas clouds at speed, collection scoops
wide open, processing systems running flat out. Purity standards are
"whatever comes out the other end." The Rim's gas refineries prioritize
throughput over quality — five hundred cargo of roughly-processed gas
is worth more than two hundred cargo of pristine fractions when you're
supplying frontier fuel depots. Speed 2 lets the Lungful follow
gas clouds as they drift, maintaining continuous collection without
the repositioning delays that slow competitors.

ships.name: Mace
ships.description: Crimson assault cruiser. Takes capital ships by force. The Fleet's heavy boarding platform.
ships.lore:
Mace cruisers carry the first boarding detachments large enough to have
their own armorers, surgeons, and prize officers. The clamp galleries are
buried behind the forward belt so the ship can stay attached under fire,
while the sickbay opens directly onto the return passage. Commanders value
Mace captains who bring back both the prize and enough marines to take the
next one.

ships.name: Magnate
ships.description: Faction flagship for the boss who outgrew borders — forged from the best of all five empires: Crimson fury-plate, Voidborn null-matter shields, Solarian logic cores, Nebula optics, Rim dark matter. Heavily armored, properly armed, and rigged so the leader who runs the whole operation can fly it into the fight himself. One per faction, keyed to the leader's hand.
ships.lore:
The empires have sovereigns. These people pay them taxes — most years, on the
profit they choose to declare — and then go on running the economy the sovereigns
merely tax. A Magnate is what that kind of money builds when it stops pretending
to respect a border. There is no empire stamp on the hull because there is no one
empire in it: the plating is Crimson fury-temper, the shields hang off Voidborn
null-matter matrices, the brain is Solarian logic stacked behind Nebula optics, and
the whole thing is laced with Rim dark matter, because the owner could afford to buy
the best of each and the freight to carry it home. It takes a faction with a holding
in every empire's space to even source one — which is precisely the point, and
precisely who flies it. It is built to go to war: against rival magnates, against
the pirates who mistake it for cargo, against the empires themselves when the math
finally favors it. The yards build exactly one per faction and key it to the boss's
own hand. You do not lead from a station chair forever. Eventually you buy the
front of the line.
ships.prestige_lock: Locked: prestige hull reserved for the leader of a faction that has earned the "Imperial Footprint" achievement.

ships.name: Mandate
ships.description: Crimson patrol enforcer. Significantly overgunned for law enforcement. Nobody complained.
ships.lore: A mandate is not a request. The Crimson Fleet's patrol vessel carries two autocannons and enough armor to shrug off return fire — considerably more combat capability than any empire's patrol doctrine calls for. When the Solarian Confederacy formally protested that the Mandate-class exceeded treaty limits for law enforcement vessels, the New Pact responded that the guns were "inspection equipment" and the armor was "weather protection." The integrated scanner is technically functional. Checking your documentation is a formality that occurs after the autocannons have already made their point. The official hail is one word: "Halt."

ships.name: Manifest Destiny
ships.description: Outer Rim exploration cruiser. The ship that goes where maps end.
ships.lore:
The Manifest Destiny is the Outer Rim's dedicated deep-space
exploration platform, designed for pilots who believe the galactic edge
is where interesting things start, not where they end. Speed 3 and
fuel-efficient engines give it the range to reach regions that exist
only as blank spots on other empires' charts. Anomaly detection and
survey instruments come standard — the Rim builds exploration ships
to find things, not just fly past them. Two scrapguns handle whatever
was already living in the blank spot. Every Manifest Destiny that
returns brings stories. Not all of them return.

ships.name: Manifold
ships.description: Voidborn mining capital. Extracts resources from parallel dimensional layers. Harvests ore, gas, and ice simultaneously.
ships.lore:
The Manifold-class extracts resources from parallel
dimensional layers that other empires cannot perceive, let alone reach.
Two thousand shield points protect against dimensional stress during
sustained multi-layer extraction operations. Nine utility slots
accommodate the most advanced sensor and extraction systems the
Collective has ever produced. The Manifold can extract ore, gas, and
ice simultaneously from overlapping dimensional layers — a capability
unique to this vessel. The Collective claims the Manifold
"accelerates resource regeneration" in depleted fields by pulling
matter through dimensional rifts. Other empires' physicists consider
this claim impossible. The resources appear anyway.

ships.name: Marauder
ships.description: Crimson weaponized gas processor. Refines volatiles into fuel, explosives, and chemical weapons components.
ships.lore:
The Marauder-class refines volatile gases into three categories
the Crimson Fleet cares about: fuel for the fleet, explosives for
ordnance, and chemical components for weapons systems. The refinery
processes run at temperatures and pressures that violate every other
empire's safety standards, which the Fleet considers a competitive
advantage. Two weapon mounts protect gas processing operations in
contested nebulae — the Fleet learned that losing a full cargo of
refined volatiles to a pirate raid is more expensive than the guns.

ships.name: Margin
ships.description: Nebula courier. Balanced speed, range, and cargo for the routes that pay on time.
ships.lore: The Federation operates a galaxy-spanning courier network, and the Margin-class is the hull they trust with the contracts that have penalty clauses.
